profile.feeling: Curiosity — or, with the right tone, surprise and protest.

examples.tr: Would you like something to eat?
examples.py: Nǐ xiǎng chī diǎnr shénme ma?

phrases.meaning: what brings you here? (to an unexpected visitor)

synonyms.nuance: shá: northern colloquial ‘what’
written ‘what’: 何时 (when), 为何 (why)

etymology.text: A corruption of medieval 是物 (‘what’) or 什物 (‘miscellaneous items’), perhaps influenced by 何物 (‘what’).

funFacts: Taiwan usually writes 什麼 or 甚麼; both are traditional forms of 什么.
pitfalls: No 吗 with a 什么 question: 你喝什么？ — with 吗, 什么 means ‘anything’: 你喝什么吗？ ‘Will you drink anything?’
Word order does not change: put 什么 where the answer goes (你喝什么？— 我喝茶).
subtleties: Before a noun, 什么 asks ‘what kind / which’: 什么菜？ ‘what dish?’.
In fast speech it is often shéme.

override.pinyin: pinyin: Mainland dictionaries (Xiandai Hanyu Cidian) give nǎ·li with a toneless li; Wiktionary’s own entry lists this toneless variant ‘nǎli’, which the kaikki extraction garbles into “nálǐ] → nǎli (toneless final syllable variant)”, so the tool cannot match it. Everything else checked clean before this override was added.

profile.feeling: Asking for a place; and the classic modest reply to praise.

senses.def: (哪里哪里) not at all — a modest reply to a compliment

examples.text: 哪里哪里，我的中文还不好。
examples.tr: Not at all, my Chinese is still not good.
examples.py: Nǎli nǎli, wǒ de Zhōngwén hái bù hǎo.

synonyms.nuance: nǎr: the erhua form — everyday in Beijing and the north
‘what place’ — a little more explicit
written ‘where’

etymology.text: 哪 (‘which’) + 里 (‘place; inside’): ‘which place’.

funFacts: Answering a compliment with 哪里哪里 literally asks ‘where? where?’ — as if the praised quality cannot be found.
pitfalls: No 吗 with 哪里: 土豆在哪里？ (not *…吗？).
哪里 nǎli (where?) vs 那里 nàli (there): only the 口 radical and the tone differ.
Say 在哪里 for ‘where is’ — the verb 在 is needed: *土豆哪里？
subtleties: Both 哪里 and 哪儿 are standard: -儿 forms (哪儿, 这儿, 那儿) are typical of Beijing and the north, -里 forms of the south, Taiwan and writing.
Spoken: the 3rd tone of 哪 before 里 is usually heard as náli.

profile.feeling: Asking about a person — at the door, on the phone, in a crowd.

senses.def: (with 都 / 也) anyone, everyone; (with a negation) nobody

phrases.tr: lù sǐ shéi shǒu — at whose hand will the deer die?
phrases.meaning: who will win in the end?

synonyms.nuance: nǎ wèi: ‘which person’ — the polite ‘who?’: 您是哪位？ ‘who is speaking, please?’
shénme rén: ‘what person, what kind of person’ — can sound suspicious

etymology.text: Phono-semantic compound: semantic 言 ‘speak’ + phonetic 隹. Cognate with the classical 孰 ‘which one; who’ (Schuessler).

funFacts: To ask a stranger who they are, 您是哪位？ is polite; 你是谁？ can sound blunt.
Like Russian кто-то / никто, Chinese makes ‘everybody / nobody’ from ‘who’: 谁都 ‘everybody’, 谁都不 ‘nobody’.
pitfalls: No 吗 with 谁: 他是谁？ — 他是谁吗？ is wrong.
谁 stays where the person would stand in the answer: 谁要咖啡？— 我要咖啡; 你找谁？— 我找老师. Nothing moves to the front.
subtleties: Two readings: shéi (everyday) and shuí (careful or formal speech); both are correct.
With 都 it means ‘everyone’: 谁都喜欢他 ‘everyone likes him’.

profile.feeling: A key on the table, a phone ringing — whose is it?
profile.synonymsNone: There is no other everyday word: ‘whose’ is always 谁 + 的, just as ‘my’ is 我 + 的.

etymology.text: 谁 ‘who’ + 的, the particle of ownership (S06): ‘who’s’.

funFacts: Chinese makes ‘whose’ the way it makes ‘my’: 我的 ‘my’, 你的 ‘your’ — 谁的 ‘whose’.
pitfalls: 谁的 comes before the noun: 谁的书？ — never *书谁的？
No 吗: 这是谁的？ is already a question.
subtleties: 谁的 can stand alone at the end: 这是谁的？ ‘whose is this?’ — answer 是我的 ‘it’s mine’.

profile.feeling: Plans and appointments: when do we eat, when are you coming?

synonyms.nuance: jǐ diǎn: ‘what time (by the clock)?’ — 你几点吃早饭？
nǎ tiān: ‘which day?’
héshí: written ‘when’

etymology.text: 什么 ‘what’ + 时候 ‘time’: literally ‘what time’.

funFacts: Chinese ‘when?’ is literally ‘what time?’ — English keeps ‘what time?’ for the clock, Chinese uses it for every ‘when’.
pitfalls: 什么时候 stands before the verb, not at the end: 你什么时候来？ — not *你来什么时候？
It only asks. ‘When I come …’ in a statement is …的时候 (S18), not 什么时候.
subtleties: For the clock time Chinese asks 几点: 你几点吃早饭？; 什么时候 can be a day, a year or a time.

profile.feeling: Asking for the way to do something — or, with surprise, ‘how come?!’.

senses.def: how? in what way? (before a verb)

examples.tr: How do you get to school?

phrases.tr: zěnme bàn — how to handle it?

synonyms.nuance: zěnyàng: ‘how, in what way’ — a little more written
rúhé: written ‘how’: 如何学习中文
zǎ: northern colloquial ‘how, why’

etymology.text: 怎 ‘how’ + the suffix 么, as in 什么 and 这么.

funFacts: 怎么 + 不 turns ‘how’ into ‘how come’: 你怎么不吃？ is surprise, not a request for a method.
pitfalls: 怎么 + verb asks for the way: 怎么去？ ‘how do I get there?’; 怎么 + 不 / 没 asks ‘how come’: 你怎么没来？
‘How are you?’ is not *你怎么？ — say 你好吗？ or 你怎么样？
subtleties: 怎么 vs 为什么: 怎么 shows surprise or disapproval (‘how come?!’), 为什么 asks neutrally for the reason.
In fast speech it is often zěm.

profile.feeling: Asking for an opinion or a state: how is it, what is it like — and ‘how about …?’.

senses.def: how? how is …? what is … like?
(不怎么样) not up to much

examples.tr: Let’s have tea — how about it?
This film isn’t up to much.

synonyms.nuance: rúhé: written ‘how (is it)’ — 你觉得如何？
zǎyàng: northern colloquial ‘how’s it?’

etymology.text: 怎么 ‘how’ + 样 ‘manner, appearance’: ‘in what manner’.

funFacts: 最近怎么样？ ‘how are things lately?’ is the friendly greeting among people who know each other — 你好吗？ is more textbook.
pitfalls: 怎么样 is the predicate itself: 这个怎么样？ ‘how is this?’ — it does not go before a verb; for the way of doing something use 怎么 + verb.
subtleties: After a suggestion it asks for agreement: 我们走，怎么样？ ‘let’s go, OK?’.

profile.feeling: Curiosity about reasons — the favourite word of every three-year-old.

synonyms.nuance: zěnme: ‘how come?!’ — surprise or reproach
gànmá: ‘what for? why on earth?’
wèihé: written ‘why’

etymology.text: 为 wèi ‘for’ + 什么 ‘what’: ‘for what’.

funFacts: 为什么 is ‘for what’ — built like Greek γιατί (για + τι ‘for what’) and English ‘what for’; Turkish neden is ‘from what’ (ne + -den).
pitfalls: 为什么 stands before the verb or opens the sentence: 你为什么不吃？ / 为什么你不吃？ — not at the end.
The answer starts with 因为 ‘because’ (S18).
subtleties: 为 is read wèi (4th tone) here, not wéi.

override.pos: Chinese grammars (现代汉语词典) class interrogative 多少 as a pronoun (代词), like 几 and 什么; Wiktionary files the same interrogative sense under “adj” (‘(interrogative) how many; how much’).

profile.feeling: Shopping and counting — any number, big or small.

examples.tr: How many students does your school have?
I know a little about it.

synonyms.nuance: jǐ: ‘how many’ when a small number (under about ten) is expected; it needs a measure word

etymology.text: 多 ‘many, much’ + 少 ‘few, little’: ‘(is it) much or little?’.

funFacts: ‘How many’ is literally ‘many-few’: the question names both ends of the scale.
多少钱？ ‘how much money?’ is the first sentence most visitors learn in a Chinese market.
pitfalls: After 多少 the measure word may be left out (多少人, 多少书); after 几 it may not (几个人).
No 吗: 这里有多少人？
subtleties: As a question word the second syllable is toneless (duōshao); in the sense ‘more or less’ it is duōshǎo.

profile.feeling: A small number expected: a child’s age, the people in a family, the time on the clock.

senses.def: how many? (a small number is expected; with a measure word)

examples.tr: How many children do you have?
How old are you? (to a child)

examples.py: Nǐ jiā yǒu jǐ kǒu rén?
examples.tr: How many people are there in your family?

examples.py: Wǒ mǎi le jǐ ge píngguǒ.

synonyms.nuance: duōshao: any number, also large ones; the measure word is optional

etymology.text: Traditional 幾: an ideogrammic compound of 𢆶 ‘silk threads; little things’ + 戍 ‘to guard’ — watching over fine details. The simplified 几 is also an old character of its own, ‘small table’.

funFacts: The simplified 几 is also an old character of its own, ‘small table’ — still heard in 茶几 chájī ‘coffee table’.
pitfalls: In everyday speech 几 takes a measure word: 几个人, 几本书 — not *几书.
Ask a child 你几岁？, but an adult 你多大？ (or politely 您多大年纪？) — 几岁 to an adult sounds as if you think they are small.
subtleties: In statements 几 means ‘a few’: 我有几本书 ‘I have a few books’.
Time and dates use 几: 几点 ‘what time’, 几号 ‘what date’, 星期几 ‘what weekday’.

profile.feeling: Choosing among things you can see or name: which one?

synonyms.nuance: shénme + noun asks ‘what (kind of)’; 哪 + measure word asks ‘which one’ of a set

etymology.text: Written 那 before the 20th century. Generally considered a fusion of 奈何 ‘how’ (Wang 1990; Sun 1992).

funFacts: Until the 20th century ‘which’ was written 那, like ‘that’; the modern 哪 adds 口, the radical of many spoken little words (吗, 呢, 吧).
pitfalls: 哪 nǎ ‘which’ vs 那 nà ‘that’: the tone and the 口 radical make the difference.
Before a noun 哪 needs a measure word: 哪本书 — never *哪书.
subtleties: In speech 哪 + measure word is often něi: 哪个 něige.
No 吗 with 哪: 你要哪个？

lexemes.role: the formal measure word for people with a role or profession — in news, reports and official numbers: 一名医生, 三名工人, 二十名学生; not for close family, and never for yourself in a polite introduction (我是医生)

profile.feeling: A white coat in a busy Chinese hospital — a respected, trusted profession.

examples.py: Zhè wèi yīshēng zài yīyuàn gōngzuò.
examples.tr: This doctor works at the hospital.

synonyms.nuance: dàifu: ‘doctor’, especially in the north and as a form of address: 王大夫
yīshī: ‘physician’ — the professional title on documents

etymology.text: 医 ‘medicine; to heal’ (traditional 醫: phonetic 殹 + semantic 酉 ‘liquor’) + 生 ‘person (of a calling)’, as in 学生.

funFacts: China has two kinds: 西医 ‘Western-medicine doctor’ and 中医 ‘doctor of traditional Chinese medicine’.
pitfalls: Do not use 位 for yourself: 我是医生 ‘I am a doctor’ — not *我是一位医生.
看医生 ‘look at the doctor’ means to see a doctor as a patient.
subtleties: A doctor is addressed as 医生 or 大夫, or surname + 医生 / 大夫: 李医生.

override.measure: measure: 位 (polite), 个 (everyday) and 名 (formal, official counts) are all standard Mandarin measure words for people in a profession; Wiktionary lists only 名 for 护士, but 位 is just as standard (一位护士), and it must not be drilled as wrong.

profile.feeling: Care and patience on the hospital ward.

synonyms.nuance: báiyī tiānshǐ: ‘angel in white’ — praise for nurses and medical staff
hùgōng: a care assistant, not a trained nurse

etymology.text: 护 ‘to protect, to look after’ (traditional 護: semantic 言 + phonetic 蒦) + 士 ‘person (of a skill)’.

funFacts: Hebrew calls a nurse אָחוֹת ‘sister’, German Krankenschwester ‘sick-sister’; Chinese 护士 is ‘the one who looks after’ — no sister at all.
pitfalls: The second syllable is toneless: hùshi.
subtleties: 护士 is used for men too; to stress it, 男护士 ‘male nurse’.

profile.feeling: Bridges, machines, software — the people who build modern China.

examples.tr: My older brother is an engineer.

examples.text: 这位工程师在这里工作。
examples.py: Zhè wèi gōngchéngshī zài zhèli gōngzuò.
Tā shì yì míng ruǎnjiàn gōngchéngshī.

synonyms.nuance: jìshùyuán: technician — a lower qualification
chéngxùyuán: programmer

etymology.text: 工程 ‘engineering; a project’ (工 ‘work’ + 程 ‘measure, procedure’) + 师 ‘master, expert’.

funFacts: 师 ‘master’ marks skilled professions: 老师 teacher, 厨师 cook, 律师 lawyer, 工程师 engineer.
pitfalls: 工程 alone means ‘a project, construction work’ — the person is 工程师.
subtleties: 高级工程师 ‘senior engineer’ is an official professional title in China.

profile.feeling: Taxis, buses and lorries — someone at the wheel.

senses.def: (slang, 老司机) an old hand, an experienced person

examples.tr: My father is a taxi driver.

examples.text: 他是老司机，什么都知道。
examples.py: Tā shì lǎo sījī, shénme dōu zhīdào.
examples.tr: He’s an old hand — he knows everything.

phrases.meaning: an experienced person, an old hand (online also with a risqué undertone)

synonyms.nuance: jiàshǐyuán: driver, pilot — the official word
shīfu: ‘master’ — how drivers and craftsmen are addressed: 师傅，去机场。

etymology.text: 司 ‘to be in charge of, to operate’ + 机 ‘machine’: ‘the one who operates the machine’.

funFacts: In a taxi you say 师傅 ‘master’ to the driver, not 司机.
pitfalls: ‘I drive (a car)’ is 我开车 (S13), not *我是司机 — 司机 names the driver of a vehicle, usually as a job.
Address a driver as 师傅, not 司机.
subtleties: 老司机 began as ‘experienced driver’ and became internet slang for ‘old hand’.

profile.feeling: Flames and woks in a restaurant kitchen.

examples.tr: He is a cook at the restaurant.
I want to be a chef.

examples.text: 这位厨师做的菜很好吃。
examples.py: Zhè wèi chúshī zuò de cài hěn hǎochī.
examples.tr: The dishes this chef makes are delicious.

synonyms.nuance: dàchú: ‘chef, big cook’ — admiring
chúzi: ‘cook’ — homely, a little rough
chuīshìyuán: cook in an army unit or canteen

etymology.text: 厨 ‘kitchen’ (traditional 廚: semantic 广 + phonetic 尌) + 师 ‘master’.

funFacts: The same 厨 is in 厨房 ‘kitchen’ (S12).
pitfalls: 厨师 is the person; ‘to cook’ is 做饭 (S07): 我妈妈做饭 — she is not a 厨师 unless it is her job.
subtleties: A famous chef is praised as 大厨.

profile.feeling: Behind the counter of a shop or department store.

examples.text: 我姐姐在超市当售货员。
examples.py: Wǒ jiějie zài chāoshì dāng shòuhuòyuán.
examples.tr: My sister works as a shop assistant at the supermarket.
The shop assistant says this one is good.

collocations.tr: to work as a shop assistant

synonyms.nuance: diànyuán: shop employee — the modern everyday word
yíngyèyuán: counter staff (shops, banks, phone companies)
xiāoshòu: salesperson; sales (as a department)

etymology.text: 售 ‘to sell’ + 货 ‘goods’ (traditional 貨: phonetic 化 + semantic 貝 ‘shell, money’) + 员 ‘staff member’.

funFacts: -员 makes staff words: 服务员 waiter, 售货员 shop assistant, 演员 actor.
pitfalls: 售货员 is the job title; in a small shop you call out 你好 or 老板 ‘boss’, not 售货员.
subtleties: 售货员 is the standard job title; in everyday talk people also say 店员, or 销售 for sales staff.

profile.feeling: Factories, building sites — work with the hands.

examples.text: 这个工厂有五百名工人。
examples.py: Zhège gōngchǎng yǒu wǔbǎi míng gōngrén.
examples.tr: This factory has five hundred workers.

synonyms.nuance: yuángōng: employee, staff (any kind of work)
láodòngzhě: labourer, working person
dǎgōng de: someone working a (temporary) job

etymology.text: 工 ‘work’ (a pictogram of a tool) + 人 ‘person’.

funFacts: 工人 and 农民 ‘workers and peasants’ appear together in Chinese political language: 工农.
pitfalls: 工人 is a manual or factory worker; an office employee is 员工 or 职员.
subtleties: In Hong Kong and Singapore 工人 also means a live-in domestic helper.

profile.feeling: Rice fields, villages, the work of the seasons.

examples.text: 这个村子的农民种水稻。
examples.py: Zhège cūnzi de nóngmín zhòng shuǐdào.
examples.tr: The farmers of this village grow rice.

examples.py: Hěn duō nóngmín qù chéngshì dǎgōng.
examples.tr: Many farmers go to the cities to work.

synonyms.nuance: nóngfū: farmer, peasant — in stories
nóngchǎngzhǔ: farm owner (a large farm)

etymology.text: 农 ‘agriculture’ (traditional 農: originally 林 ‘vegetation’ + 辰 ‘hoe’ — clearing weeds) + 民 ‘people’.

funFacts: 农民工 ‘peasant-workers’ are the hundreds of millions of rural people who work in Chinese cities.
pitfalls: 农民 is the rural farming population — a social group (‘peasant’); a Western-style farm owner is 农场主.
subtleties: 农 is in 农村 ‘the countryside’ and 农业 ‘agriculture’.

profile.feeling: Order on the street; the number to call is 110.

examples.tr: That police officer is over there.

synonyms.nuance: jǐngguān: police officer — also a respectful form of address
mínjǐng: ‘people’s police’ — the ordinary mainland police officer
tiáozi: ‘cop’ — rude

etymology.text: A modern word borrowed in writing from Japanese 警察 keisatsu; 警 ‘to warn, be alert’ + 察 ‘to examine’.

funFacts: 警察 came into Chinese from Japanese (keisatsu), like many modern words written with Chinese characters — 经济 ‘economy’, 社会 ‘society’.
pitfalls: 警察 is both the person and the force: 他是警察 ‘he is a policeman’, 叫警察 ‘call the police’.
subtleties: The police emergency number in mainland China is 110.

profile.feeling: Contracts, courts, careful words.

examples.tr: My older sister is a lawyer.

examples.py: Tā qǐng le yí ge lǜshī.

synonyms.nuance: fǎlǜ gùwèn: legal adviser (of a company)
dàlǜshī: barrister (Hong Kong)

etymology.text: 律 ‘law, rule’ (semantic 彳 + phonetic 聿) + 师 ‘master, expert’.

funFacts: In Buddhism 律师 once meant a master of the monastic rules (the vinaya) — long before it meant ‘lawyer’.
pitfalls: Pinyin lǜ keeps the two dots: l + ü (lü), different from lù.
subtleties: 律 also means ‘rule, regularity’: 规律 ‘a law (of nature)’.

profile.feeling: Studios, galleries, creative freedom.

examples.tr: I want to be an artist.

synonyms.nuance: huàjiā: painter
yīnyuèjiā: musician
gǎo yìshù de: ‘someone who does art’ — casual, sometimes ironic

etymology.text: 艺术 ‘art’ (艺 ‘skill’ + 术 ‘technique’) + 家 ‘specialist, -ist’.

funFacts: 家 ‘home’ also makes experts: 画家 painter, 作家 writer, 科学家 scientist, 艺术家 artist.
pitfalls: 艺术家 is a big word for an established artist; for a hobby say 他喜欢画画 ‘he likes painting’.
subtleties: Polite measure words suit it best: 一位艺术家, 一名艺术家.
